Project Parallax research draft: megalithic acoustics, granite impedance, and structural resonance

This document is an internal research draft. It uses only the supplied dataset. Numerical values below are not independent field measurements of megaliths, and they are not treated as archaeological fact.

Reported acoustic-transmission context

The dataset indicates that an arXiv-linked source was found. The supplied excerpt concerns extraordinary acoustic transmission in a single slit by boundary impedance engineering. Extraordinary acoustic transmission is commonly associated with periodic or multi-aperture structures. The study reports that a single subwavelength slit can support strongly enhanced transmission when its boundary response is described by an effective impedance, and that a reduced analytical model is used. The excerpt is truncated after that clause; this draft does not complete or invent the remainder of that paper.

Illustrative granite-impedance framing

The quantitative rows in the dataset are labeled illustrative_model, not literature-sourced megalith data. The model note states that the figures follow the standard acoustic impedance mismatch equation (Z1-Z2)^2/(Z1+Z2)^2, and that a fabricated piezoelectric charge calculation was identified as unsubstantiated and removed. Under that model, a frequency of 115.0 Hz is associated with an acoustic pressure of 28.98879093718812 Pa, an energy reflection of 99.98755114530057 percent, and a boundary status of HIGH_REFLECTION_BARRIER.

Those values are consistent with a large impedance contrast in ordinary airborne-to-solid mismatch physics. They are not presented here as evidence that granite architecture was intended as an acoustic device, nor as a measurement of any specific monument.

Limits on megalithic interpretation

Questions about structural resonance in stone remain open in this draft. The skeptic critique supplied with the dataset states that the high acoustic energy reflection figure is standard impedance physics, not archaeological proof of intent, and that airborne acoustic waves alone cannot overcome stone mass without an additional coupling mechanism such as seismic strain or a closed Helmholtz geometry. This draft treats that caution as binding on interpretation.
